body.text: Bullying and sexual harassment claims among 3,000 complaints at big four firms
Australia's big four accounting firms — Deloitte, PwC, KPMG and EY — were the subject of more than 3,000 complaints over three years.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said the complaints included serious allegations of bullying and sexual harassment, but firms shut down staff and whistleblowers who tried to make complaints.
In the wake of the KPMG audit leaks scandal and subsequent parliamentary probe, ASIC investigated the big four about how they handled internal whistleblower complaints.
In its review, it found that between July 1, 2023, and June 26, 2026, there were 3,215 total internal complaints recorded among the big four.
Over a wider timeframe, 558 were audit complaints provided to ASIC.
The regulator said of these, it identified 35 that raised issues related to the conduct of an audit or the misuse of audit client information.

ASIC's review follows whistleblower revelations that at KPMG confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus, and that the firm then mishandled the whistleblower's complaint about it.
In the wake of the saga, the federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February.
Audit staff told to stay quiet
The most common concerns involved audit work that had been falsified, inaccurately documented or recorded without adequate evidence.

A number of complaints alleged that employees were directed to "disregard, conceal or not escalate issues identified during an audit" or that, when escalated, the issues were not investigated appropriately.

"They also alleged that staff were told not to report identified discrepancies, to pass audit testing despite concerns, or not to raise issues with an engagement partner or other senior personnel," the review said.

A "small number" of complaints involved possible manipulation of audit sampling. They included allegations that audit samples were removed or replaced, or that changes were proposed without an adequate audit basis.
"This conduct can undermine the reliability of the audit evidence, bias the testing results, and affect the auditor's conclusions,"
the review said.

The review also found "misuse of statutory audit client information and other breaches of confidentiality, data security or independence requirements, and retaliation against, or victimisation of, reporters who raised issues in connection with a statutory audit".

ASIC said in a number of complaints the firms had no records indicating that concerns about the audit quality had been fully examined. It said audit concerns were often treated by firms as workplace matters.
Allegations of bullying and sexual harassment
ASIC said it heard another 523 complaints that included a range of wider issues not related to audit, including allegations of bullying and sexual harassment.
There were also complaints raised about how firms handled sensitive information, including those sent to personal email accounts.
"These stakes are really high," ASIC commissioner Kate O'Rourke told ABC News.
"The firms … audit most of the 94 per cent of listed companies by market capitalisation and the vast majority, 85 per cent, of registrable superannuation entities."
She said audit firms were "gatekeepers to Australia's financial markets" and needed to be "carefully and really thoroughly interrogating complaints that they've received internally".
ASIC has come under fire from whistleblowers for being too slow to act, with one whistleblower claiming the regulator has to be "dragged kicking and screaming" to investigate misconduct allegations.
ASIC chair Sarah Court has previously told parliament that the watchdog required greater powers to investigate and prosecute the big four.
ASIC's review noted that "some of the complaints included serious allegations of misconduct that are under consideration for enforcement action".

"There have also been other issues identified which relate to matters already under investigation by ASIC, including several matters which have been referred for consideration as part of our existing investigations into KPMG about misstatements in transparency reporting," the review said.

Ms O'Rourke said ASIC was engaging with accounting lobbies including Chartered Accountants and CPA Australia, as well as the Tax Practitioners Board, "on matters involving their members that may raise concerns about breaches of professional or ethical standards".
Firms vow to encourage 'speak-up culture'
The big four all vowed to do better when it came to investigating complaints and dealing with whistleblowers.

A spokeswoman for KPMG Australia said since the KPMG audit leaks saga, the firm had initiated an "action plan" and was "strengthening whistleblower protections and improving how we identify, manage and respond to complaints".
"We are also progressing a number of measures to further strengthen our speak-up culture,"
she said.

A PwC Australia spokeswoman said, "audit quality remains our highest priority" and the firm was also committed to "embedding a strong speak-up culture, which has been one of the key focus areas of our reforms since 2023".
Deloitte's spokeswoman said the firm had "long invested in a strong speak-up culture as foundational to a strong ethical culture".

"As noted in the ASIC report, complaint numbers are not directly comparable as firms with a stronger speak-up culture, or more comprehensive processes for identifying and recording complaints, may report higher numbers,"
she said.
A spokesman for EY said the firm had put in "robust processes for complaints handling across the firm and publicly discloses its complaints overview and outcomes annually".
Call to split firm functions

On Friday, a host of ASIC representatives including its chair Sarah Court and executive director of enforcement and compliance, Chris Savundra, will be brought before the KPMG inquiry to answer questions about how it handles whistleblower complaints.
Labor senator Deborah O'Neill, who chairs the inquiry, said ASIC's review of the big four showed a "shameful list of failures".
"It's clearer than ever that the barrel contains more than just a few bad apples,"
she said.
"This report confirms what we've found repeatedly through our work. Again and again, these massive opaque partnerships show contempt for the standards that apply to the rest of corporate Australia.
"I'm especially concerned that matters relating to audit quality were treated as workplace or bullying complaints and swept under the carpet."
Greens Finance and Public Service spokesperson senator Barbara Pocock said the allegations of sexual harassment and bullying were "concerning".
"There are complaints relating to whistleblowers not being treated seriously, which is also concerning,"
Senator Pocock said.

While ASIC has received evidence of thousands of complaints by the workers at the big four firms, she said "the regulator lacks the power to hold these big partnerships to account except in relation to senior auditors as individuals".

"That's why we need to subject these massive partnerships to the same rules of tax, transparency and whistleblowing as other large entities through corporations law, separate the functions of audit from non-audit and regulate them properly, and ban unethical contractors from government work," she said.
